To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the in vitro genetic toxicity assays can be used in conjunction with in vivo studies and other information, such as structure, to identify carcinogens, but the results are not unambiguous.
• The in vitro tests currently used in genetic toxicology cannot be used to identify all rodent carcinogens, but they can be used to identify many rodent carcinogens.

(1) in vitro tests can be used to identify rodent carcinogens that are trans-species carcinogens and (2) the in vitro results for rodent carcinogens are not sufficiently concordant to allow the use of these tests to unambiguosly define carcinogens.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of in vitro assays to identify carcinogens and to understand the relationship of these assays to carcinogenesis.
the identification of the minimum number of short-term tests that can be used to discriminate between rodent carcinogens and non-carcinogens.
the development of a rational basis for the use of short-term genetic toxicity tests.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the in vitro genetic toxicity assays are not predictive of carcinogenicity.
in vitro genetic toxicity tests can be used to identify potential human carcinogens, but the tests must be used in the context of the overall weight of evidence for carcinogenicity.
the in vitro assays cannot be used to identify all carcinogens and non-carcinogens.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have not yet reached the point at which we can unambiguously predict the carcinogenicity of a chemical based on its in vitro mutagenic activity.
we need more data and better models.
the in vitro assays are not sufficiently predictive to be used in isolation to identify all potential human carcinogens.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are no simple rules that can be applied to predict carcinogenicity from short-term tests.
the short-term test results should be used in conjunction with other information, including structural alerts and other in vivo and in silico data, to make decisions regarding human exposure.
we should be cautious in applying short-term genetic toxicity results to predict carcinogenic potential, but that there are many chemicals for which the in vitro data provide useful information.
